## Hard-to-vary report: "Does willpower mindset really moderate the ego-depletion effect?"

**1. The question, frozen.** The article answers several questions; the title makes one central: *does willpower mindset (believing willpower is limited vs. not) moderate the ego-depletion effect, such that only limited-mindset people show depletion?* Range: one lab, one depletion task (letter cancelation), one outcome task (Stroop), students, tested once. Kind of question: mostly *what produces it* — does the manipulation produce worse Stroop performance, and more so for one mindset? A second, quieter question rides along: *what can we tell from what we see* about Job et al.'s original report. Two nested jobs: (a) the overall depletion effect, (b) its moderation.

**2. The parts** (authors' own terms): the two preregistered hypotheses; the design changes (frequent manipulation-check ratings, no blurred text in the depletion condition, vocal Stroop, an added extension block, reversed rating scale); the shifted analysis (fixed-effects then mixed-effects, no unmotivated covariates); the sample size; the exclusions; the manipulation-check results; the review of 13 related studies; and the catch-all "any of the changes we introduced may have led to the failure."

**3. Part by part.** No totals.

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Depletion manipulation moved effort/difficulty/tired ratings | **Held** | By the difference-score tests and the MANOVA; running the study without the manipulation would move these numbers. (The MANOVA was added after the fact.) |
| No depletion effect on Stroop, Blocks 1 and 2, errors and RT | **Two routes** | Reached by fixed-effects and by mixed-effects, with and without extreme-RT trimming. Neither needs the other alone. |
| The one significant interaction (Block 1 errors, B=.875, p=.038) is not a replication | **Held** | By the sign (nonlimited mindsets, not limited) and by its loss when one outlier goes (p=.162). Both halves are checkable. |
| "The original HLM did not nest trials" | **Held** | By the reported df in the original (t(1433) against 1,440 trials) — an arithmetic check on someone else's paper. |
| Underpowered for d≈.41 | **Held** | By the power calculation; it is a stated limit, arrived at openly. |
| The candidate causes of the null (frequent ratings, no blurred text, different analysis) | **Loose** | Swap any one for any other and the null is covered equally well. What all three share: *some deviation from Job et al.'s procedure*. That general part, not any named one, is what is doing the work. |
| "Job et al.'s finding is not a replicable finding" | **Borrowed** | Rests on a qualitative review of 13 studies and the authors' companion paper, neither tested here. |
| Sample size rule of thumb, preregistered exclusions | **Fixed** | Set by the owners before data; not tested. Two criteria were then dropped after seeing the data. |
| Whether the original's own analysis would reproduce its pattern | **Unknown** | Models did not converge; the original dataset was refused. Reanalysing that dataset would settle it. |
| Trait self-control null | **Held**, with the study-wide power caveat attached to it | It was tested, fixed and mixed effects. |

**4. Whole-explanation checks.**
- *Flip.* Had the moderation appeared, the same account would have read the design changes as improvements. So the "our changes may have caused it" story covers both outcomes — the signature of a loose part. The authors say as much.
- *Direction.* No reverse running: they refuse to conclude from their own null, and lean on other studies instead. Correctly identified as a "what can we tell" answer.
- *Answer hidden in the starting points.* "Unconventional," "theoretically unmotivated covariates," "artificial laboratory settings," "not validated as measures of self-control" carry verdicts inside descriptors. Preregistration-plus-data-sharing is offered as the discriminator between studies that found the effect and those that did not.
- *Pairs that pull.* (i) "The manipulation worked" (check ratings) against "the manipulation did nothing" (Stroop). The outcome wins; the check is demoted to exploratory. (ii) "Underpowered" against "the finding is not robust" — a null this study cannot trust is still used as the study's main product. (iii) "Changes improved the design" against "changes may explain the failure."
- *Catch-all and gauge.* "Any of the changes we introduced may have led to the failure" is a catch-all. The gauge exists — run the same protocol with and without the frequent ratings, or with blurred vs. crisp text in the depletion condition — and is not read; the authors argue it is not worth running. A catch-all with an unread gauge makes the account easier to vary.
- *Change list.* Well covered on the outcome side (condition × mindset × block × trial type × errors/RT × transformations). What it leaves out openly: no real-life setting, no alternate depletion task.
- *Best rival.* "The effect is real, small, and this study is too small to see it." No change on this list separates that rival from the authors' reading; other large studies also lack power for a non-crossover moderation, so it stays open.
- *Where the parts came from.* Design and analysis: **built** — justified step by step, so they can be caught out. Sample size: **fitted** to a previous study's habit, and asserted in the preregistration. The robustness verdict: **borrowed** from a literature review. The catch-all: **asserted**.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.** One poke would do most: keep everything else identical and vary only the frequency of the manipulation-check ratings — if the null survives both, "participants were alerted" stops doing work. The second: blurred vs. crisp text in the depletion condition, which would either hold Job's conjecture or kill it. Either turns a swappable story into a testable part.

**6. What this does not show.** A tight handle is not truth, and a loose one is not error. This study's null does not make Job et al.'s effect false; a full-power null would not have made it false either. Nothing here rules on whether willpower mindset is a useful idea — the authors say so themselves.

**7. One next step.** Pick one loose candidate and run its poke. The blurred-text comparison is the cheapest, and it is the one the original authors themselves named.
